Program Overview
The Interdisciplinary Materials Science is designed for students who want flexibility and breadth in their graduate education. Students create individualized Ph.D. or M.S. programs by selecting from a wide variety of courses across Chemistry, Physics, Medicine, and all Engineering departments. This interdisciplinary structure encourages collaboration and supports research across topics such as new materials, energy, and computational modeling.
Watch the IMS Program Video
IMS Program Information
Graduate Student Handbook - IMS Policies & Expectations
The IMS Graduate Student Handbook is designed to complement the regulations of the Vanderbilt Graduate School and the School of Engineering. It provides additional guidance on program policies, expectations, and resources. Please note that specific research paths, requirements, and expectations may also be set at the discretion of your research advisor.
Research Rotations - Explore Before You Commit
A hallmark of the IMS program is the opportunity for first-year students to complete three research rotations before selecting a permanent advisor. Each 10-week rotation provides hands-on experience in a different lab, with about 9 hours per week devoted to research.
Rotations allow students to:
Explore diverse research areas
Build relationships with multiple faculty mentors
Identify the best fit for long-term doctoral work
At the end of each rotation, students submit a short report, written in the style of a conference paper, summarizing their research. This ensures valuable experience in both conducting and communicating science from the very beginning of graduate training.
Professional Development - Resources for Success
During their first semester, all incoming IMS students are required to participate in the Professional Development Seminar Series. While this is not a registered course, attendance at all sessions is expected unless an excused absence is approved.
The seminar series is designed to help students build the skills and habits that contribute to long-term success in graduate school and beyond. Topics typically include:
The role of a graduate student
Rotations 101
Mindfulness & wellness
Building self efficacy
Making the most of your TA experience
How to make a research poster
Communication conflict
Presentation skills
What makes a successful graduate student
Rotation reports and scientific writing
How to read a scientific paper
Work/Life balance
Current Students - Meet Current Ph.D. Candidates
Huijin 'Ginny' An
Thesis Advisor: Sharon Weiss (Electrical and Computer Engineering) & Andrea Locke (Biomedical Engineering)
Research: Optical biosensors are powerful analytical instruments to measure biomolecular interactions in real-time, label free. My research is focused on development of paper-based porous silicon biosensor that can be functionalized by diverse molecules for sensing specific diseases, using reflectance measurement to achieve label free detection and quantitative analysis. Ultimate goal of my research is designing an optical biosensor which can be used at the point of care.
Undergraduate: Incheon National University, Nano Bioengineering
Thiago Arnaud
NSF GRFP Fellow & Provost's Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisor: Joshua Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: As technology continues to decrease in size, their optical and thermal bottlenecks in performance increase. My research focuses on studying materials that support polaritons, quasiparticles of light and matter, that are both confined and propagate on the nanoscale. In particular, I am interested in pushing the length scales at which we can control polaritons and leverage them as a novel thermal transport mechanism.
Undergraduate: University of Florida, Physics
Emma Bartelsen
Thesis Advisor: Joshua Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering) & Shekhar Bhansali (Electrical and Computer Engineering)
Research: I specialize in electromagnetic energy at the nano- to atomic-scale and the interactions between light and matter in confined systems. My research focuses on designing tunable Tamm-plasmon-based thermal emitters for gas sensing applications, including the detection of greenhouse gases and pollutants. I developed a filterless non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) sensing approach that enhances sensitivity by targeting multiple absorption bands simultaneously, enabling the detection of gases like propane, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide with high selectivity and reduced fabrication complexity. Expanding beyond environmental applications, I am working to create compact, non-invasive breath analysis tools to improve diabetes management, combining optics, photonics, and material science to address critical challenges in healthcare and the environment.
Undergraduate: University of Kansas, Mechanical Engineering
Laura Bergemann
Dean's Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisors: Katie Van Schaik (Radiology & Radiological Sciences) & James Crowe (Pediatrics, Pathology, Microbiology, Immunology)
Research: Mummies provide valuable insights into human health throughout history. My research focuses on studying mummified remains using CT scans and ancient DNA analysis to investigate diseases, injuries, genetic traits, and lifestyle factors in past populations. By combining imaging and molecular techniques, this work aims to reconstruct patterns of health over time and improve our understanding of medicine and the history of disease.
Undergraduate: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Chemistry
Masters: New York University, Conservation of Historic and Artistic Works & History of Art and Archaeology

Dakota Braaten
Thesis Advisor: Deyu Li (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: I specialize in nanoscale heat transport and understanding phonon-polariton heat transfer in low-dimensional materials. My work focuses on engineering materials to increase the thermal conductivity and reduce the thermal contact resistance between nanofillers in polymer composites using non-equilibrium phonon polaritons. In addition to this work with phonon-polaritons, I have worked on studying the oxidation effects on quasi-1-dimensional (quasi-1D) thermal transport in van der Waals materials to determine the origin of the quasi-1D confinement effect in thin nanomaterials. Ultimately, I want to design next-generation polymer composites and better understand the thermal physics that lead to quasi-1D thermal transport.
Undergraduate: Kansas State University, Chemical Engineering
Jeb Buchner
University Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisor: Joshua Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: Infrared light has a host of applications from molecular sensing, to thermal imaging, to communications. However, its large wavelength prevents it from being effectively integrated into on-chip devices, as it requires larger components. By harnessing strong material responses from phonons, we can effectively bypass this limit. In particular, I am investigating how we can use 2D materials in various stacking and twisted arrangements to control IR light at the nanoscale using the additional degrees of freedom these materials provide. My work includes simulation, fabrication, and characterization of these materials and devices.
Undergraduate: Auburn University, Materials Engineering
Emily Byrum
Thesis Advisor: David Kosson (Civil and Environmental Engineering) and Florence Sanchez (Civil and Environmental Engineering)
Research: Geopolymers are a low carbon alternative to Ordinary Portland Cements (OPCs). My research is on the creation of geopolymers for nuclear waste containment with a focus on 3D printing. OPC cement is commonly used in nuclear waste containment and has two major drawbacks, a high carbon footprint and poor performance at high temperatures. The goal of this research is to create a geopolymer cement that is a low carbon alternative to OPC that can be mass produced via 3D printing to lower the industry's carbon footprint and to be more effective at nuclear waste containment.
Undergraduate: Arizona State University, Biophysics
Jongha Choi
University Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisor: Josh Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: From the heat radiated by a microchip to the way light carries information on a photonic chip, controlling light at scales far below its own wavelength is one of the central challenges of modern nanophotonics. My research focuses on hyperbolic phonon polaritons, hybrid light–matter waves that emerge when mid-infrared light couples to atomic vibrations in van der Waals crystals such as α-MoO₃, squeezing and steering light at the nanoscale. By engineering the underlying substrate and the twist angle between stacked crystal layers, I work to actively control how these polaritons propagate and even reverse their direction. I combine near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM) and infrared nano-spectroscopy with electromagnetic simulations to understand and design these systems, toward reconfigurable mid-infrared technologies for sensing, thermal management, and on-chip optical signal processing.
Undergraduate: University of California, Los Angeles, Chemistry & Materials Science
Masters: University of California, Los Angeles, Chemistry
Emmanuel Dabuo
Thesis Advisor: Joshua Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering) & Mona Ebrish (Electrical and Computer Engineering)
Research: For decades, silicon has been the cornerstone of the semiconductor industry. However, Silicon has been pushed to its limit in terms of its applications in high frequency, high power and high voltage devices. This has shifted the attention of scientists and researchers to the field of wide bang gap semiconductor materials. A critical challenge in advancing these materials is understanding and controlling defects, which directly impact device performance and reliability. My research focuses on developing advanced, non-destructive techniques, Infrared Scattering Scanning Nearfield Optical Microscopy (s-SNOM) and Nanoscale Fourier Transform Infrared (Nano-FTIR) Spectroscopy, to characterize defects in wide band gap semiconductors at the nanoscale. These methods overcome the diffraction limit, enabling spatial resolutions far beyond conventional optical techniques. As semiconductor devices continue to shrink, even a single defect can drastically alter functionality. By providing new insights into defect characterization, this research aims to support the growth of high-performance, next-generation semiconductor technologies.
Undergraduate: University of Education, Winneba, Physics
Sariah D'Empaire-Salomon
NSF GRFP Fellow & Provost's Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisor: Douglas Adams (Civil Engineering) & Tonia Rex (Ophthalmology & Visual Science)
Research: Primary blast injury remains poorly characterized, particularly in how blast overpressure interacts with the skull, brain, and sensory pathways. My research focuses on developing biofidelic human head and eye surrogates using soft polymer tissue components. These models are used to study how primary blast waves propagate through cranial structures and sensory pathways, generating injurious pressures and strains. By combining materials characterization, embedded sensing, and controlled blast testing to evaluate PPE designs This work aims to advance physiologically relevant primary blast injury metrics that guide improved protective systems for warfighters and first responders.
Undergraduate: Livingstone College, Biology
Katelyn Derr
Thesis Advisor: Leon Bellan (Mechanical Engineering) ) & Dolly Ann Padovani-Claudio (Department of Ophthalmology, University of Michigan)
Research: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a microvascular complication of diabetes and a leading cause of blindness in working-age adults. Increased levels of pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic factors have been shown to correlate with DR progression. My research focuses on developing a microfluidic model to mimic retinal microvasculature to investigate the role of this chemokine signaling in retinopathy pathophysiology. My work consists of fabricating a microfluidic hydrogel device, 3D cell culture, and a wide array of imaging and molecular biology characterization approaches to help gain a deeper understanding of retinopathy pathophysiology.
Undergraduate: University of South Carolina, Biomedical Engineering
Elizabeth Hays
NSF GRFP Fellow & University Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisor: Janet Macdonald (Chemistry)
Research: My research investigates phase control of colloidal metal chalcogenide nanocrystals, which have phase dependent magnetic, electronic, and optical properties. Chalcogenide precursor reactivity is a powerful handle we have to target certain crystalline phases. While plenty of sulfur precursors with varying decomposition rates and routes on metal centers have been used in phase control studies, tellurium precursors are notoriously uncooperative and prefer to decompose to unreactive Te(0) intermediates. In an effort to target specific metal telluride phases colloidally, I am synthesizing a family of organotelluride precursors with varying reactivities. The goal of my research is to access desirable metal telluride phases colloidally, which requires less energy input compared to conventional synthetic methods like chemical vapor deposition.
Undergraduate: Murray State University, Biochemistry

Research: My research interest is computational material science, studying materials properties computationally using tools like DFT and MD Simulations. I'm part of the National Science Foundation Center for Chemical Innovation 'The MXenes Synthesis, Tunability and Reactivity (M-STAR)'. My research focuses on exploring 2D transition metal carbides/nitrides (MXenes) using DFT. Specifically, I am investigating hybrid organic-inorganic MXenes, where the organic surface terminations can significantly alter the properties of these 2D materials and pave the way for further reactions.

Jack Loken
NSF GRFP Fellow
Thesis Advisor: John Wilson (Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering) & Jonathan Brunger (Biomedical Engineering)
Research: Recent developments in cell-based immunotherapies like chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells have greatly improved the treatment of hematologic malignancies, such as leukemia and lymphoma. These approaches typically require isolating a patient’s cells and engineering them to more selectively and robustly target cancer. Current cellular immunotherapies target proteins displayed by cancer cells, but these markers are often present at other locations in the body leading to off-target cytotoxicity. My focus is on designing materials that can interact with engineered cells to impart greater targeting capabilities and decrease off-target activation and background signaling. I am working to synthesize polymers that display small molecules recognized by engineered cells to induce antitumor signaling at various sites of interest for immunotherapy. My approach consists of reversible addition-fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) polymerization for polymer synthesis, synthetic biology techniques for cell design, and in vivo analysis of polymer kinetics and therapeutic efficacy in various tumor models.
Undergraduate: University of Wisconsin – Madison, Mechanical Engineering
Mackey 'Trey" Long III
GEM Fellow & Dean's Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisor: Joshua Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: My research explores how phonon polaritons—hybrid light-matter excitations formed by the coupling of infrared electromagnetic fields to polar lattice vibrations—mediate heat transport at the nanoscale. While conventional thermal radiation is governed by Planck’s law in the far field, materials separated by sub-micrometer distances can exchange energy through near-field electromagnetic modes that far exceed blackbody limits. I study these effects theoretically and experimentally in solid-state systems, with an emphasis on understanding how polaritonic modes propagate, couple across interfaces, and contribute to thermal energy transfer. By investigating the heat transport properties of phonon polaritons, my work aims to advance nanoscale thermal management and enable new approaches for thermophotovoltaics, heat-assisted magnetic recording, nanolithography, and reliable integrated circuits and NEMS devices.
Undergraduate: Auburn University, Materials Science and Engineering
Mark Mc Veigh
Thesis Advisor: Leon Bellan (Mechanical Engineering) & Todd Peterson (Physics & Astronomy)
Research: Positron emission tomography (PET) is an incredibly powerful diagnostic procedure that holds the potential for clinicians to track virtually any biological process using specific radiotracers. There have been thousands of radiotracers developed but due to the high cost of synthesis, clinicians rely on only one radiotracer for over 95% of PET scans. I am working on developing a microfluidic synthesis platform that will reduce the cost of radiotracer production and employ a dose-on-demand methodology, allowing clinicians to choose the radiotracer that best suits the needs of the patient. The platform uses inexpensive microfluidic chips that contain multiple channels and chambers to execute all necessary synthesis steps. By optimizing the chip architecture and implementing automated fluidic handling, we are working towards being able to synthesize any radiotracer rapidly and inexpensively.
Undergraduate: Northeastern University, Chemical Engineering
Masters: Northeastern University, Chemical Engineering
Owen Meilander
Thesis Advisor: Mona Ebrish (Electrical and Computer Engineering)
Research: To deal with the growing power demand, high efficiency power electronics are needed. While silicon devices are highly matured, in high power applications their intrinsic material properties lead to large devices with significant ant power losses. Wide bandgap (WBG) semiconductors, such as gallium nitride (GaN), promise up to a 1000x increase in efficiency at high voltages, but material defects have limited the advancement of these devices. My research focuses on the identification of defects in GaN through the use of spectroscopic techniques and fabrication of GaN devices. My work will help to correlate these defects to device operation, resulting in more efficient and reliable devices.
Undergraduate: Westminster College, Physics & Mathematics
Vivian Nwosu-Madueke
Thesis Advisor: Carlos Silvera Batista (Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering)
Research: My research focuses on the electrokinetic behavior of colloidal particles driven out of equilibrium by applied electric fields. I investigate how particle properties, including surface chemistry, charge, geometry, and material composition, govern processes such as polarization, fluid flow, particle motion, and collective assembly. A central aspect of my work is understanding how ion transport near particle surfaces couples with electric fields to generate propulsion and interparticle interactions. Using experimental measurements of particle dynamics, surface properties, and frequency-dependent electrical response, I identify the mechanisms that control these behaviors and determine how they can be tuned. This research contributes to the broader understanding of active and field-responsive colloidal systems and supports the development of design principles for reconfigurable materials, microscale transport, and controlled self-assembly.
Undergraduate: University of Lagos, Chemistry
Johanna Pearson
Provost's Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisor: Leon Bellan (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: In 2023, nearly 7 million Americans were diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease (AD). With no cures currently available and the number of patients diagnosed expected to increase with a growing elderly population, there is a clear need to develop new treatments. However, efforts to develop these treatments are hindered by the fact that current animal and human tissue slice models of AD have numerous ethical and practical limitations. This is the motivation behind my research; I focus on developing an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived model of neurovascular coupling (NVC). NVC refers to the complex signaling process employing neurons, glial cells, mural cells, and endothelium to link lumen diameter of blood vessels (and thus local blood flow) to nearby levels of neuronal activity. In AD there is a disruption of this signaling pathway which results in notable cognitive impairment. A patient-specific, engineered model of NVC could serve as a powerful platform to facilitate development of pharmacological treatments for NVC dysfunction.
Undergraduate: Case Western Reserve University, Neuroscience
Antony Peng
NSF GRFP Fellow
Thesis Advisors: Matthew Day (Physics & Astronomy) & Josh Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: As quantum technologies become increasingly prevalent, it is more important than ever that we have a greater understanding of how we can control quantum systems and how these small-scale interactions amount to macroscopic properties. Currently, my work focuses upon employing infrared polaritonics and interfacial interactions between two-dimensional materials as a potential method for altering and controlling ground-state phenomena of quantum systems. This can be exploited to shift the potential energy landscape of materials with congested phase diagrams to access normally inaccessible ground-state properties such as superconductivity and ferroelectricity.
Undergraduate: Vanderbilt University, Chemistry
Masters: Columbia University, Chemistry
Ke-Sean Peter
IBM Fellow
Thesis Advisor: Joshua Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering) & Sharon Weiss (Electrical and Computer Engineering)
Research: Quantum computers hold promise in bringing vast improvements to computation, allowing new discoveries in fields from medicine to materials. Current technology requires quantum computers to be run at extremely cold temperatures. My research focuses on developing sources of optical qubits, using nanofabrication techniques, wide band-gap semiconductors, photoluminescence microscopy and single photon detection techniques, so that room temperature operation of quantum computers may be realized.
Undergraduate: Grambling State University, Chemistry & Mathematics & Physics
Courtney Ragle
Thesis Advisors: Lauren Buchanan (Chemistry) & Josh Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: My work takes place within the infrared region of the electromagnetic spectrum, where vibrational and phonon polaritons (quasi-particles melding together light and matter) flourish. These polariton systems show promise for understanding and manipulating molecular dynamics within organic materials and biologically relevant molecules, as well as exploring polariton assisted nanoscale energy transfer. I work to create cavity systems with decreasing mode volumes to enhance energy transfer and push into the ultra-strong coupling regime. The studies employ two-dimensional infrared spectroscopy (2DIR) and scattering near-field optical microscopy (SNOM) as the main instruments of exploration.
Undergraduate: Fort Lewis College, Chemistry
Emanuela Riglioni
Thesis Advisor: Sharon Weiss (Electrical and Computer Engineering)
Research: Quantum photonics offers significant potential for enabling next-generation quantum technologies, such as quantum communication, quantum computing, and quantum sensing. A central challenge in this field is the development of efficient, scalable, and integrable photonic platforms that operate in the telecommunication band. My work focuses on the design and development of nanophotonic components, as well as on gaining a deeper understanding of the underlying physical mechanisms governing their behavior, with the goal of advancing applications in quantum technologies and telecommunications.
Undergraduate: Xavier University of Louisiana, Chemistry
Jose Rosario Figueroa
First-year student
Undergraduate: Inter American University of Puerto Rico, Electrical Engineering
Masters: North Carolina State University, Nanoengineering
Rahul Shah
Thesis Advisor: Jason Valentine (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: The modern world is driven by an insatiable demand for detailed information. From understanding the complex interplay of proteins in medical diagnosis, to identifying early onset of plant diseases for agriculture, spectral information is a game changer. This is my research. I aim to develop next-generation Hyper-spectral Imaging Spectrometers with cutting-edge metasurfaces. My work includes theoretical modelling and simulations, to hands on fabrication and characterization, using the tools available to me through VINSE.
Undergraduate: Indian Institute of Science - Bangalore, Materials Science
Masters: Indian Institute of Science - Bangalore, Materials Science
Robert Shields
IBM Fellow
First-year student
Undergraduate: University of California Santa Barbara, Physics
Soren Smail
NSF GRFP Fellow & Dean's Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisor: Sharon Weiss (Electrical and Computer Engineering) & Paul Laibinis (Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering)
Research: The need for rapid, low-cost biosensors with high sensitivity and specificity is becoming increasingly apparent for applications ranging from disease diagnosis and monitoring to environmental and food safety. Porous silicon (PSi)-based optical biosensors offer a promising platform for these needs, as they enable real-time measurement of biomolecular interactions without the use of external labels (e.g., fluorescent or enzymatic tags). My research focuses on chemical surface modifications to PSi which provide selective biorecognition capabilities while simultaneously preventing non-specific adsorption of unwanted proteins, cells, and other contaminants. By improving the signal-to-noise ratio in complex biological samples, this work advances the development of highly sensitive rapid diagnostics which can be used at the point-of-care.
Undergraduate: University of Cincinnati, Biochemistry
Carson Snow
Dean's Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisor: Jason Valentine (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: My research focus is on the inverse design of metasurfaces, where computational methods are used to optimize feature geometries that produce specific optical behaviors. This approach provides a way to design complex optical encoders by directly training and simulating the response of the metasurface. The designs can then be prepared for fabrication, with the goal of creating metasurfaces that can be integrated into intelligent imaging systems. Through this process, I am studying how such devices might contribute to compact optical components for tasks in imaging and computer vision, especially in settings where hardware and computational resources are limited.
Undergraduate: Colorado School of Mines, Engineering Physics
Andrew Steiner
NSF GRFP Fellow & University Graduate Fellow
Thesis Advisor: De-en Jiang (Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering)
Research: Designing better functional materials, like those for energy storage and catalysis, requires a detailed understanding of their underlying structure, yet the experimental techniques that probe this, such as X-ray diffraction and neutron vibrational spectroscopy, often produce data that is difficult to interpret. My research aims to solve this problem, developing computational framework solutions that bridge atomistic simulation and measured data, reducing the analytical load on the experimentalist. I am currently working on two projects. The first is an inverse structure solution approach from X-ray diffraction data, ideal for samples containing novel structures that do not exist in any crystallographic database and therefore cannot be solved by conventional matching methods. The second is developing the first open-access simulated spectral database for interpreting neutron vibrational spectra of MXene catalysts, providing experimentalists with quantitative insights into surface structure and composition that were previously inaccessible.
Undergraduate: University of Florida, Materials Science and Engineering
Maxwell Ugwu
Thesis Advisors: Justus Ndukaife (Electrical and Computer Engineering) & Joshua Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: My research is focused on nanoparticle trapping and spectroscopic study with nanotweezer devices. Our objective is to create innovative technologies that will enable single nanoparticle trapping and analysis, with a particular focus on nanoplastics and extracellular vesicles (EVs). These tools will enhance the study of extracellular vesicles (EVs) by offering precise and reliable analysis, facilitating their integration into clinical diagnostics for breakthroughs in early disease detection and improved patient outcomes. Beyond medicine, they hold significant potential for environmental applications, enabling accurate detection and characterization of nanoplastics, advancing monitoring efforts, and informing strategies to mitigate pollution.
Undergraduate: Caritas University, Nigeria, Chemistry
Masters: University of Nigeria, Physical Chemistry
Matthew Vasuta
Thesis Advisors: Kane Jennings (Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering) & Shihong Lin (Civil Engineering)
Research: Distillation has dominated the separation of organic mixtures for decades despite its high thermal energy requirement. In an effort to reduce this impact, I work on synthesizing polymer thin films that act as distillation substitutes by separating water from a polar organic at cooler temperatures. The synthesis method we employ in my lab is unique as it uses a catalyst-laden substrate to spin coat and polymerize the film at the same time, allowing us to create films in minutes with very minimal solvent. This versatility makes it so a variety of different films with various functionalities can be quickly synthesized for water-polar organic separation, each with exciting compositional, wetting, environmental, and separating properties.
Undergraduate: University of Tennessee - Knoxville, Chemical Engineering
Harrison Walker
NSF GRFP Fellow
Thesis Advisors: Sokrates Pantelides (Physics) & Josh Caldwell (Mechanical Engineering)
Research: My research focuses on predicting and interpreting phonons, the quantized atomic vibrations that govern heat transport, infrared optical response, structural phase transitions, and electron-phonon interactions in materials. I am particularly interested in materials where nanoscale structure reshapes the vibrational spectrum, including systems governed by interfaces, superlattice periodicity, polarization textures, moiré reconstruction, and nanoscale confinement. To study these effects, I develop and apply computational methods that connect atomistic dynamics to vibrational electron energy-loss spectroscopy in the monochromated transmission electron microscope. My work combines density functional theory, machine-learned interatomic potentials, molecular dynamics, and multislice electron-scattering simulations to interpret experimental spectra and identify the underlying atomic motion. More broadly, I aim to build predictive tools for understanding how nanoscale structure controls material behavior relevant to thermal management, infrared nanophotonics, and future electronic technologies.
Undergraduate: Auburn University, Materials Science and Engineering
Christopher Whittington
Thesis Advisor: Sharon Weiss (Electrical and Computer Engineering)
Research: In the face of escalating data demands, electronic components alone struggle to meet society's growing data transmission needs. To overcome this challenge, we turn to the power of light – by harnessing photons, we have the potential to achieve astonishingly rapid data transmission speeds, exceeding a terabyte per second. My research is dedicated to crafting nanoscale photonic components using silicon and silicon nitride. These components find applications in optical filters, switches, and the promising realm of photonic-based quantum computing.
Undergraduate: Clark University, Physics
Career Outcomes - Where our Graduates Work
Our interdisciplinary approach prepares IMS graduates for diverse and rewarding careers. By working across engineering, physics, chemistry, and medicine, students gain marketable skills that translate to success in academia, industry, and government.
42% of graduates enter industry – companies include Johnson & Johnson, Dow, DuPont, Exxon, and biotech start-ups.
35% pursue careers in academia – from research universities to teaching institutions.
23% serve in government – including the FDA, NIH, and the U.S. Patent Office.

Apply to our graduate program
Master of Science
The M.S. degree requires a minimum of 24 hours of formal coursework beyond the bachelor’s degree, plus a thesis approved by two faculty members. Students must also complete at least 6 hours of graduate research. The thesis is defended publicly, but no qualifying exam is required. Coursework must include at least three of the four IMS core program courses.
Doctor of Philosophy
The Ph.D. degree requires a total of 72 credit hours, including at least 24 hours of formal coursework. Of those, 15 hours must come from the IMS core, with courses selected across five fundamental areas. All IMS students must take Atomic Arrangements, plus one course from three of the four remaining areas. Core courses must be completed with a grade of B or higher, and taken the first semester in which they are available.
Core courses
The core consists of:
Materials Fundamentals
- IMS 6310 Atomic Arrangements in Solids
Research Rotations
- IMS 6391/92 Research Rotations
Three courses from three of the four areas below:
Solid State Materials
One of the following:
- EECE 6301 Solid-State Materials
- EECE 6306 Solid-State Effects and Devices I
- ME 8364 Nanophotonic Materials
- PHYS 5640 Physics of Condensed Matter
Statistical Mechanics & Thermodynamics
One of the following:
- CHBE 6110 Advanced Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics
- CHEM 5350 Statistical Thermodynamics
- ME 8320 Statistical Thermodynamics
- PHYS 5200 Statistical Physics
- PHYS 8040 Statistical Mechanics
Quantum
One of the following:
- CHEM 5320 Quantum Chemistry
- PHYS 5651 Advanced Quantum Mechanics
- PHYS 8030 Quantum Mechanics
- PHYS 8152 Quantum Mechanics of Solids
Chemistry
One of the following:
- CHEM 5040 Nanoparticles
- CHEM 5150 Electrochemistry: Theory and Analysis
- CHEM 5340 Applications of Group Theory
- CHEM 5410 Molecular Modeling Methods
- CHEM 5420 Computational Structural Biochemistry
- CHEM 5610 Chemistry of Inorganic Materials
- CHEM 5620 Chemistry of Biological Materials
- CHEM 5630 Macromolecular Chemistry
- ME 8321 Spectroscopic Methods
The remainder of the 72 hours can be taken as dissertation research, coursework, or transfer credit (if applicable). Performance in dissertation research does not affect the student’s GPA. However, it is critical to note that until 72 hours is reached that a full 9-credit hours are taken each semester. This may be all in research, all in courses and seminar, or some combination thereof.
Elective Courses
ll students are required to take 9 credit hours of elective courses. These can be selected from any courses within the School of Engineering or Science-related Graduate classes within Arts & Sciences. Additional courses taken within a single core focus area listed above (e.g., CHEM 5610 and 5040) will qualify as electives. Financial Aid
IMS offers full support for Ph.D. candidates through scholarships, fellowships, teaching assistantships (TAs), and research assistantships (RAs).
Support includes:
Annual stipend starting at $40,000 (2026–2027 TA/RA award)
100% tuition scholarship
100% health insurance coverage
100% student activity and recreation fees
Additional competitive fellowships of $1,000–$10,000 per year for top applicants
First-year Ph.D. students are typically supported as TAs before moving to RAs. TA assignments generally involve teaching Strength of Materials in the fall and Materials Science I in the spring. Applicants are encouraged to pursue external fellowships and grants.
